claim: Current models assume that commands that hold the limb at a target location do not depend on the commands that moved the limb to that location.
source: Current models assume that commands that hold the limb at a target location do not depend on the commands that moved the limb to that location.
evidence: This is stated as a description of current models in the abstract, and is supported by citations to existing literature in the introduction.

claim: On a within-trial basis, the commands that hold the arm and finger at a target location depend on the mathematical integration of the commands that moved the limb to that location.
source: on a within-trial basis, the commands that hold the arm and finger at a target location depend on the mathematical integration of the commands that moved the limb to that location.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from monkeys and humans shown in Figures 1-7.

claim: Following damage to the corticospinal tract, both the move and hold period commands become more variable.
source: Following damage to the corticospinal tract, both the move and hold period commands become more variable.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from stroke patients shown in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: Following damage to the corticospinal tract, the hold period commands retain their dependence on the integral of the move period commands.
source: However, the hold period commands retain their dependence on the integral of the move period commands.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from stroke patients shown in Figure 7F, H, I, and J.

claim: The postural controller possesses a feedforward module that uses move commands to calculate a component of hold commands.
source: Thus, our data suggest that the postural controller possesses a feedforward module that uses move commands to calculate a component of hold commands.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, based on inference from the observed integration relationship.

claim: The computation of hold commands from move commands may arise within an unknown subcortical system that integrates cortical commands to stabilize limb posture.
source: This computation may arise within an unknown subcortical system that integrates cortical commands to stabilize limb posture.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the stroke patient data showing preserved integration despite cortical damage.

claim: Current models assume that movement and postural controllers are independent.
source: This architecture (Figure 1A, left) in which movement and postural controllers are independent is implicit in optimal control formulations of reaching (Yadav and Sainburg, 2011; Lametti et al., 2007; Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Ghez et al., 2007) and forms the basis for interpreting how neurons in the motor cortex encode reach kinematics (Sachs et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on optimal control models of reaching.

claim: A feedback controller generates commands that move the arm, and then upon reach end, a postural controller holds the limb still.
source: In current models (left), a feedback controller generates commands that move the arm, and then upon reach end, a postural controller holds the limb still.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A (left panel).

claim: In the oculomotor system, the hold controller's output directly depends on the move controller.
source: In order to hold the eyes at a target, the oculomotor system uses a hold controller whose output directly depends on the move controller (Cohen and Komatsuzaki, 1972; Cannon and Robinson, 1987; Crawford et al., 1991; McFarland and Fuchs, 1992; Miri et al., 2011; Shadmehr, 2017; Godaux et al., 1993; Cheron et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies of the oculomotor system.

claim: The oculomotor move controller produces commands that displace the eyes.
source: The move controller produces a set of commands that displace the eyes (Shadmehr, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to existing literature.

claim: Move commands in the oculomotor system are integrated in real-time by a distinct brainstem structure, yielding sustained commands that hold the eyes and head still when movement ends.
source: Simultaneously, these commands are integrated in real-time by a distinct brainstem structure, yielding sustained commands that hold the eyes and the head still when the movement ends (Cohen and Komatsuzaki, 1972; Miri et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of the oculomotor system.

claim: Total inhibition of the mouse motor cortex during reaching causes the arm to stop moving, but the muscles continue to receive commands that hold the arm steady against gravity.
source: total inhibition of the mouse motor cortex during reaching causes the arm to stop moving, but the muscles continue to receive commands that hold the arm steady against gravity (Guo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Damage to the brainstem structure that holds the eyes produces nystagmus.
source: whereas damage to the brainstem structure that holds the eyes produces nystagmus (Kaneko, 1997; Kaneko, 1999), we know of no condition that resembles nystagmus in the context of reaching.
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The integral of reach activity predicted hold activity after movement ended when monkeys reached to a single target from various directions.
source: When monkeys reached to a single target from various directions, we found that the integral of reach activity predicted hold activity after the movement ended.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The same integration function accounted for hold period activity at various endpoints as target location varied.
source: Furthermore, as the target location varied, the same integration function accounted for hold period activity at the various endpoints.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Across a range of directions and endpoints, the hold period activity was related, through integration, with the preceding move period activity.
source: Thus, across a range of directions and endpoints, the hold period activity was related, through integration, with the preceding move period activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the monkey reaching experiments.

claim: During goal-directed finger movements with constant start and end target locations, there was natural variability in muscle activity both during movement and during the ensuing hold period.
source: As monkeys flexed their finger, there was natural variability in muscle activity both during the movement and during the ensuing hold period.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: On a within-trial basis during finger movements, changes in hold period commands in all recorded muscles were correlated with the integral of the preceding commands that had brought the finger to its current location.
source: However, this variability had structure: on a within-trial basis, changes in hold period commands in all recorded muscles were correlated with the integral of the preceding commands that had brought the finger to its current location.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Altering reach commands through adaptation in humans caused changes in hold period commands on a within-trial basis.
source: To do this, we altered the reach commands of humans through adaptation (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3-6.

claim: As reach period commands changed during adaptation, the entire postural field shifted, indicating that changes to reach commands altered the null point of the hold controller.
source: We found that as the reach period commands changed, the entire postural field shifted, indicating that changes to reach commands altered the null point of the hold controller.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The function that related the hold period controller to the preceding reach period was the same integration function observed in point-to-point reaching and finger movements.
source: Notably, the function that related the hold period controller to the preceding reach period was the same integration function that we had observed in point-to-point reaching and finger movements.
evidence: This is a summary statement connecting findings across different experimental paradigms.

claim: Stroke survivors with damage to the corticospinal tract above the brainstem exhibited large trial-to-trial variability in commands during both reach and hold periods.
source: As expected, these stroke survivors exhibited large trial-to-trial variability in the commands that they produced during both the reach and the subsequent hold periods.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In stroke survivors, the link between move and hold period commands appeared intact: on a within-trial basis, hold period forces were related via integration to the immediately preceding reach period forces.
source: Remarkably, the link between move and hold period commands appeared intact: on a within-trial basis, the hold period forces were related via a form of integration to the immediately preceding, but now imperfect, reach period forces.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In monkeys, healthy humans, and stroke survivors, across arm movements and finger movements, the hold period commands depended on the preceding commands that had moved the limb to its current location.
source: Thus, in monkeys, healthy humans, and stroke survivors, across arm movements and finger movements, the hold period commands depended on the preceding commands that had moved the limb to its current location.
evidence: This is a summary of findings across all experimental populations and paradigms.

claim: The postural controller possesses a subcortical feedforward module that calculates hold period commands through real-time integration of move period commands.
source: These results raise the possibility that the postural controller possesses a subcortical feedforward module that calculates hold period commands through real-time integration of the move period commands.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The feedforward computation of hold commands combines with visual and proprioceptive feedback to produce sustained commands that result in postural stability.
source: This feedforward computation then combines with visual and proprioceptive feedback to produce the sustained commands that result in postural stability.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Monkeys made reaching movements in the vertical plane to one of eight targets.
source: We used intramuscular electrodes to measure activity of 20 shoulder and elbow muscles during point-to-point reaching in the vertical plane (nine muscles in monkey A, 11 muscles in monkey B). On each trial, monkeys first moved their hand from a central location to one of eight targets, held their hand at that target for at least 0.5 s, then reached back to the central location and again held their hand for at least 0.5 s (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and is supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Activity of 20 shoulder and elbow muscles was measured during point-to-point reaching (nine muscles in monkey A, 11 muscles in monkey B).
source: We used intramuscular electrodes to measure activity of 20 shoulder and elbow muscles during point-to-point reaching in the vertical plane (nine muscles in monkey A, 11 muscles in monkey B).
evidence: This describes the experimental measurements.

claim: For most muscles (14/20), change in hold period activity was well predicted by the integration equation.
source: Indeed, for most muscles (14/20), change in the hold period activity was well predicted by Equation (1).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the experimental findings.

claim: When target location was constant across various movement directions, changes in hold period activities of many muscles were proportional to the integral of their respective activity during the preceding reach.
source: For example, when the target location was constant (Figure 1D, reach back) across various movement directions, the changes in the hold period activities of many muscles were proportional to the integral of their respective activity during the preceding reach (red lines, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Integration of reach period activity was a reasonable predictor of change in hold period activity across all conditions (R2 = 0.58 for Monkey A and R2 = 0.54 for Monkey B).
source: Remarkably, we found that integration of the reach period activity was a reasonable predictor of the change in hold period activity across all conditions (R2 = 0.58 for Monkey A and R2 = 0.54 for Monkey B).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Within each muscle, the integration gain k was no different for outward reaches and return reaches.
source: Within each muscle, the integration gain k was no different for outward reaches and return reaches (Figure 1G, paired t-test on single muscle regression slopes, p=0.943).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The same integration gain predicted hold activity for fast and slow movements.
source: In addition, the same integration gain predicted hold activity for fast and slow movements (Figure 1G, fast vs. slow, two-sample t-test, p=0.30) which differed modestly in terms of movement duration (two-sample t-test, p<0.001, fast movement duration of 350.3 ± 11.1 ms and slow movement duration of 453.6 ± 4.9 ms, mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A single function (Equation 1) could account for various movements and speeds, despite the differing dynamics of these reaches.
source: This indicated that a single function (Equation (1)) could account for various movements and speeds, despite the differing dynamics of these reaches.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Some muscles (6/20) did not exhibit the pattern described by Equation 1, and these muscles had little to no activity during the hold periods.
source: Notably, despite these general trends, some muscles (6/20) did not exhibit the pattern described by Equation (1). These muscles shared a specific property: they had little to no activity during the hold periods (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Equation 1 seemed to apply primarily to those muscles that modulated their activity during the hold period, contributing to maintenance of arm posture.
source: Thus, Equation (1) seemed to apply primarily to those muscles that modulated their activity during the hold period, contributing to maintenance of arm posture in this task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The gain of integration was similar for horizontal versus vertical movements.
source: However, the gain of integration was similar for the two groups of movements (Figure 1G, ANCOVA, movement type by moving EMG integral interaction effect on holding activity, F = 0.37, p=0.54).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Integration of reach period activity was a better predictor of hold period activity than either the maximum or minimum muscle activity in 17/20 muscles.
source: This alternative hypothesis also proved to be significantly less accurate than Equation (1) (within muscle comparison, paired t-test, p=0.005, Figure 1H). In 17/20 muscles, integration of the reach period activity was a better predictor of the hold period activity than either the maximum or minimum muscle activity.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: For reaching across various directions and endpoints, the change in a muscle's activity from the pre-movement hold period to the post-movement hold period was partially predicted by the integral of that muscle's activity during the intervening reach period.
source: In summary, for reaching across various directions and endpoints, the change in a muscle's activity from the pre-movement hold period to the post-movement hold period was partially predicted by the integral of that muscle's activity during the intervening reach period.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the monkey reaching experiments.

claim: Trial-to-trial variation in move period commands should lead to consistent trial-by-trial changes in subsequent hold period commands, even if the target location remains constant.
source: According to Equation (1), trial-to-trial variation in the move period commands should lead to consistent trial-by-trial changes in the subsequent hold period commands, even if the target location remains constant.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the integration hypothesis.

claim: Monkeys were trained to use their index finger to track a visual target that moved at 12 deg/sec over a 1 s period between a start (12°) and an end location (24°) against a spring load that resisted flexion.
source: Monkeys were trained to use their index finger to track a visual target that moved at 12 deg/sec over a 1 s period between a start (12°) and an end location (24°) against a spring load that resisted flexion (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At the start location, the spring load was 0.026 N⋅m, and as the finger flexed, the load increased linearly, reaching 0.048 N⋅m at the target.
source: At the start location, the load was 0.026 N⋅m. As the finger flexed, the load increased linearly, reaching 0.048 N⋅m at the target.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Muscle activity was measured using subcutaneous electrodes implanted over 17 muscles (eight muscles in monkey R, nine in monkey D).
source: We measured muscle activity using subcutaneous electrodes implanted over 17 muscles (eight muscles in monkey R, nine in monkey D).
evidence: This describes the experimental measurements.

claim: Variation in hold position accounted for less than 2% of the trial-to-trial variability in hold period EMG.
source: We found that variation in hold position accounted for less than 2% (R2 = 0.0107 ± 0.0041, mean ± SEM across all muscles in both monkeys, individual regressions for each muscle) of the trial-to-trial variability in hold period EMG
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Hold activity at the start was a rather poor predictor of hold activity at the target, accounting for about 8% (monkey R) and 7% (monkey D) of the variance in the data.
source: Overall, hold activity at the start appeared to be a rather poor predictor of hold activity at the target, accounting for about 8% (monkey R) and 7% (monkey D) of the variance in the data (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Trial-to-trial displacement explained less than 1% of the variance in both the integral of move period activity and the change in hold activity.
source: This did not appear consistent with the data: trial-to-trial displacement explained less than 1% of the variance in both the integral of move period activity (R2 = 0.006 ± 0.0018, mean ± SEM), and the change in hold activity (R2 = 0.005 ± 0.001, mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis.

claim: The integral of move period activity exhibited robust correlation with the change in hold period activity.
source: On the other hand, the integral of move period activity exhibited robust correlation with the change in hold period activity, as shown for an example recording session in the left panel of Figure 2E.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A single function accounted for approximately 50% and 40% (monkeys R and D) of the trial-by-trial variability in holding activity.
source: Thus, the gain of the integration function was similar across muscles, and a single function accounted for approximately 50% and 40% (monkeys R and D) of the trial-by-trial variability in holding activity.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Roughly 10% of the variability in the change in hold period EMG could be explained by the integral of move period activity of other muscles.
source: Roughly 10% of the variability in the change in hold period EMG could be explained by the integral of move period activity of other muscles (R2 = 0.10 ± 0.02, mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis.

claim: Move period activity in a given muscle was a much better predictor of the change in hold period activity in that same muscle than move period activity in other muscles.
source: Therefore, while some of the variance in hold period activity could be explained by the move period activity in other muscles, move period activity in a given muscle remained a much better predictor of the change in hold period activity in that same muscle (R2 = 0.42 ± 0.031, mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of statistical results.

claim: For a constant target location, on trials in which a muscle moved the finger with greater activity, it also produced greater activity during the subsequent hold period.
source: In summary, for a constant target location, on trials in which a muscle moved the finger with greater activity, it also produced greater activity during the subsequent hold period.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the finger movement experiments.

claim: About 45% of the trial-to-trial variation in the change in hold period activity could be associated with the integral of the preceding move period activity.
source: About 45% of the trial-to-trial variation in the change in hold period activity could be associated with the integral of the preceding move period activity.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Participants adapted their move period commands by reaching while holding the handle of a robotic arm that imposed a velocity-dependent force field.
source: To do this, we instructed participants to reach to a target while holding the handle of a robotic arm (Figure 3A), and adapted their move period commands by imposing a velocity-dependent force field (Albert and Shadmehr, 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: On a within-trial basis, the integral of move period force accounted for 39 ± 2% (mean ± SEM) of the variance in hold period force in the null field.
source: On a within-trial basis, the integral of move period force accounted for 39 ± 2% (mean ± SEM) of the variance in hold period force.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The gain of the integration function was the same whether or not the weight of the arm was supported by a frictionless air-sled.
source: Like the EMG patterns, the force patterns did not appear to be trivially related to biomechanical constraints imposed on the arm due to gravity: the gain of the integration function was the same whether or not the weight of the arm was supported by a frictionless air-sled (Figure 3B, two-sample t-test, p=0.90).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The relationship between move and hold period forces remained unchanged when reaches were divided into fast and slow movements.
source: Remarkably, the relationship between move and hold period forces remained unchanged when we divided the null period reaches of each subject into fast and slow movements (Figure 3D, ANCOVA, movement type by move force integral interaction effect on hold force, F = 0.007, p=0.935).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: As reach period force changed from one trial to the next during adaptation, so did the hold period force.
source: Remarkably, as the reach period force changed from one trial to the next, so did the hold period force (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: The hold period forces were not transient, but sustained, persisting up to 6 s during the entire hold period interval.
source: Notably, the hold period forces were not transient, but sustained, persisting up to 6 s during the entire hold period interval (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over the course of adaptation, Equation 2 accounted for 48 ± 3% (mean ± SEM across 32 participants) of the variance in the change in hold period forces.
source: The relationship between the change in hold period force and the (now externally-driven) reach period force was again consistent with integration: over the course of adaptation, Equation (2) accounted for 48 ± 3% (mean ± SEM across 32 participants) of the variance in the change in hold period forces.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis.

claim: As the integral of reach period forces approached zero in a bidirectional force field experiment, hold period forces gradually vanished.
source: However, this is not what we observed: as the integral of reach period forces approached zero, hold period forces gradually vanished (Figure 4B, Phase 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Even though reach period forces were matched just before the end of movement, the ensuing hold period force depended on the entire history of the reach.
source: That is, even though reach period forces were matched just before the end of movement (Figure 4C), the ensuing hold period force depended on the entire history of the reach.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was no difference in the integration function between each phase of the bidirectional force field experiment.
source: In addition, we observed no difference in the integration function between each phase of the experiment (paired t-test on slope, p=0.22, paired t-test on intercept, p=0.09).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: On a within-trial basis, as the reach period forces changed, so did the ensuing hold period forces, with the change in hold period force partially described via integration of the temporal history of the preceding reach period forces.
source: Together, these observations demonstrated that on a within-trial basis, as the reach period forces changed, so did the ensuing hold period forces. The change in hold period force was partially described via a function that integrated in time the temporal history of the preceding reach period forces.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the force field adaptation experiments.

claim: The observed trial-by-trial correlations between move activity and change in hold activity were almost entirely driven by the integration of the move commands, with little dependence on variability in the initial hold activity.
source: In summary, the observed trial-by-trial correlations between move activity and change in hold activity were almost entirely driven by the integration of the move commands, with little dependence on variability in the initial hold activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on statistical analysis of the data with restricted variance in hold 1 activity.

claim: After participants were exposed to a force field, the postural field's null position was no longer aligned with the target.
source: However, after participants were exposed to a force field, the postural field changed: the null position was no longer aligned with the target (Figure 5B, right).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The postural field's null position shifted by approximately 1 cm in the direction of the force produced during the reach.
source: Rather, it shifted by approximately 1 cm (Figure 5D; paired t-test, p<10−4) in the direction of the force produced during the reach.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The orientation and stiffness of the postural field remained unchanged after force field adaptation.
source: In contrast, the orientation (Figure 5D, paired t-test, p=0.84) and stiffness (Figure 5D, paired t-test, p=0.62) of the postural field remained unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The holding force at the hand scaled linearly with the distance between hand position and the postural null position.
source: The holding force at the hand scaled linearly with the distance between hand position and the postural null position (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The hold period forces measured in previous experiments were a proxy for the location of the null position of the postural controller.
source: This implied that the hold period forces we had measured in previous experiments (Figures 3–4) were a proxy for the location of the null position of the postural controller: the larger the hold period force at the target, the farther the null position of the postural field.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: As the reach period forces changed, the null position of the postural field shifted in the same direction as the change in the preceding move period forces.
source: Thus, as the reach period forces changed, so did postural control: the null position of the postural field shifted in the same direction as the change in the preceding move period forces.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the postural field measurements.

claim: The integrator must be adaptive: the integration function must change when there is an error between its current output and the desired movement endpoint.
source: To solve this problem, the integrator must also be adaptive: the integration function must change when there is an error between its current output and the desired movement endpoint (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the need to maintain postural stability during adaptation.

claim: Integrator adaptation would be driven by unexpected deviations from the hand's desired trajectory as the reach period ends and the hand arrives at the target location.
source: Presumably, this error-based adaptation would be driven by unexpected deviations from the hand's desired trajectory as the reach period ends and the hand arrives at the target location.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of integrator adaptation.

claim: Participants with larger endpoint errors ultimately produced smaller holding forces.
source: Critically, we found that participants with larger endpoint errors ultimately produced smaller holding forces (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: About 40% of the variability in integration gain could be explained by the magnitude of the late endpoint errors.
source: In fact, about 40% of the variability in integration gain could be explained by the magnitude of the late endpoint errors (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The adaptation of integration gain progressed over time.
source: This adaptation of integration gain progressed over time (Figure 6E, repeated measures ANOVA, F = 12.60, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In the early part of training, the integration gain was no different than that of the pre-adaptation null trials.
source: In the early part of training, the integration gain was no different than that of the pre-adaptation null trials (Figure 6E, post-hoc comparison, p=0.88).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Late in training, the integration gain had decreased substantially.
source: However, late in training, the integration gain had decreased substantially (Figure 6E, post-hoc tests, p<0.001 for comparison of late adaptation with both null field trials as well as early adaptation trials).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: As the move period commands adapt, so too must the integration function.
source: Rather, as the move period commands adapt, so too must the integration function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The adaptation of hold commands does not occur instantaneously, but appears to emerge gradually as errors near the end of the movement are experienced repeatedly.
source: Like the adaptation of movement commands, the adaptation of hold commands does not occur instantaneously, but appears to emerge gradually as errors near the end of the movement are experienced repeatedly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Stroke patients exhibited profound impairments, as demonstrated by difficulty with extension of their arm during unsupported reaching.
source: The patients exhibited profound impairments, as demonstrated by difficulty with extension of their arm during unsupported reaching (Zackowski et al., 2004; Roh et al., 2015; Figure 7A, patient S015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and citations to previous studies.

claim: Movements of the paretic arm exhibited erratic trajectories.
source: As has been noted before (Scheidt and Stoeckmann, 2007; Coderre et al., 2010), movements of the paretic arm exhibited erratic trajectories (Figure 7B)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and citations to previous studies.

claim: Movement duration increased by approximately 41% in the paretic arm compared to controls.
source: increased movement duration (paretic vs. control) of approximately 41% (paretic vs. non-paretic, paired t-test, p<0.01; paretic vs. control, two-sample t-test, p<10−4)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis.

claim: Reach endpoints terminated nearly 89% further away from the target location in the paretic arm compared to controls.
source: and reach endpoints that terminated nearly 89% (paretic vs. control) further away from the target location (paretic vs. non-paretic, paired t-test, p<0.01; paretic vs. control, two-sample t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis.

claim: The reaching impairment in stroke patients coincided with a marked increase in the trial-to-trial variability of move period forces.
source: The reaching impairment coincided with a marked increase in the trial-to-trial variability of move period forces (traces in Figure 7C solid lines; Figure 7D paretic vs. control, Wilcoxon rank-sum, p<0.001; Figure 7D paretic vs. non-paretic, Wilcoxon signed-rank, p=0.058).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The trial-by-trial variability of the hold period forces was significantly greater in the paretic arm of the patients.
source: The trial-by-trial variability of the hold period forces, like the move period forces that preceded them, was significantly greater in the paretic arm of the patients (Figure 7E; paretic vs. control, two-sample t-test, p=0.01; paretic vs. non-paretic, paired t-test, p=0.06).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In the null field trials, the coupling between move and hold periods was intact in stroke patients.
source: Remarkably, in the null field trials, the coupling between move and hold periods was intact in stroke patients (Figure 7H, paretic vs. control, two-sample t-test, p=0.14; paretic vs. non-paretic, paired t-test, p=0.63).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Despite damage to the CST, stroke patients learned to alter their move period forces during force field adaptation.
source: Because force field adaptation is largely a cerebellar-dependent process (Smith and Shadmehr, 2005), despite damage to the CST the patients learned to alter their move period forces.
evidence: This is supported by data and a citation to previous work on cerebellar involvement in adaptation.

claim: Equation 2 provided a reasonable account of the within-trial relationship between move period and change in hold period forces for the paretic arm, non-paretic arm, and dominant arm of age-matched controls.
source: Once again Equation (2) provided a reasonable account of the within-trial relationship between the move period and the change in hold period forces for the paretic arm, non-paretic arm, and the dominant arm of age-matched control subjects (paretic vs. control, two-sample t-test, p=0.08; Figure 7I: paretic vs. non-paretic, paired t-test, p=0.24).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The integration gain was not significantly different across the paretic and non-paretic limbs of the patients, nor across the patients and age-matched controls.
source: Notably, the integration gain was not significantly different across the paretic and non-paretic limbs of the patients, nor across the patients and age-matched controls (Figure 7J; paretic vs. control, two-sample t-test, p=0.86; paretic vs. non-paretic, paired t-test, p=0.91).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The integration function was similar in healthy participants and stroke patients.
source: In other words, the integration function was similar in healthy participants and stroke patients.
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical findings.

claim: Damage to the CST severely affected the reach period commands, resulting in high trial-to-trial variability.
source: In summary, damage to the CST severely affected the reach period commands, resulting in high trial-to-trial variability.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the stroke patient experiments.

claim: The change in hold period commands remained coupled to the integral of the preceding reach commands in both null field and force field trials in stroke patients.
source: However, the change in hold period commands remained coupled to the integral of the preceding reach commands in both null field and force field trials.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the stroke patient experiments.

claim: The gain of integration in stroke patients was not different than that of healthy controls, suggesting that CST damage impaired the reach commands, but not the process of integration that may have generated the hold commands.
source: The gain of this integration in the stroke patients was not different than that of healthy controls, suggesting that CST damage impaired the reach commands, but not the process of integration that may have generated the hold commands.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Current computational models of reaching view move and hold periods as events that take place in sequence.
source: Current computational models of reaching view move and hold periods as events that take place in sequence: the sensory representation of the target engages a feedback controller that moves the arm, and then once the desired endpoint has been achieved, a separate controller is engaged that produces the sustained commands that hold the arm (Yadav and Sainburg, 2011; Lametti et al., 2007; Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Ghez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of current models supported by citations.

claim: Current models have usually assumed that the motor cortex is responsible for generating the move period as well as the ensuing hold period commands.
source: These models have usually assumed that the motor cortex is responsible for generating the move period as well as the ensuing hold period commands (Humphrey and Reed, 1983; Kurtzer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a description of assumptions in current models supported by citations.

claim: The experiments suggest the possibility of a different architecture in which movement commands are integrated in real-time by a separate network of neurons of possibly subcortical origin, resulting in holding commands.
source: Here, our experiments suggest the possibility of a different architecture (Figure 7G), one in which movement commands are integrated in real-time (Figure 1B) by a separate network of neurons of possibly subcortical origin, resulting in holding commands.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Control of the arm may share a design principle present in control of the eye and the head.
source: If true, this would imply that control of the arm shares a design principle present in control of the eye (Cohen and Komatsuzaki, 1972; Cannon and Robinson, 1987; Crawford et al., 1991; McFarland and Fuchs, 1992; Miri et al., 2011; Shadmehr, 2017; Godaux et al., 1993; Cheron et al., 1986) and the head (Crawford et al., 1991; Klier et al., 2002; Shaikh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and citations to studies of eye and head control.

claim: Transient inhibition of the mouse motor cortex during reaching causes the arm to stop moving, but the muscles continue to receive commands that hold the arm steady against gravity.
source: For example, transient inhibition of the motor cortex during a reach results in 'freezing of the arm' at its current posture, and not loss of muscle tone (Guo et al., 2015). That is, despite near complete removal of output from the motor cortex during a reach, commands of unknown origin continue to sustain arm position against the force of gravity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: The model suggests that a distinct structure, possibly located in a subcortical area, integrates the cortically-generated reach commands and maintains posture despite removal of reach commands.
source: Our model suggests that a distinct structure, possibly located in a subcortical area, integrates the cortically-generated reach commands up until the moment of cortical inhibition, and thus maintains posture despite removal of reach commands.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Cortical stimulation not only moves the limb, but also produces specific postures in primates and rodents.
source: This model is also consistent with the observation that cortical stimulation not only moves the limb, but also produces specific postures in primates (Graziano et al., 2002) and rodents (Harrison et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The total displacement of the limb during cortical stimulation appears to scale with the duration of stimulation, consistent with the idea that displacement is produced due to integration of motor commands over time.
source: Moreover, the total displacement of the limb appears to scale with the duration of stimulation, consistent with the idea that displacement is produced due to integration of motor commands over time.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations from cortical stimulation studies.

claim: The idea that integration occurs outside of the motor cortex potentially explains why successful decoders of cortical activity are designed to control cursor velocity, as opposed to cursor position.
source: The idea that integration occurs outside of the motor cortex potentially explains why successful decoders of cortical activity are designed to control cursor velocity, as opposed to cursor position (Sachs et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2011; Gilja et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to brain-computer interface studies.

claim: To hold the cursor still, decoders assume that the cortex encodes a zero-velocity command rather than a position-based command.
source: To hold the cursor still, these decoders assume that the cortex encodes a zero-velocity command rather than a position-based command.
evidence: This is a description of how brain-computer interface decoders work.

claim: The cortex is primarily concerned with dynamic quantities, that is changes in the state of the limb, rather than the maintenance of a specific limb state over time.
source: This observation is consistent with the possibility that the cortex is primarily concerned with dynamic quantities, that is changes in the state of the limb, rather than the maintenance of a specific limb state over time.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Neurons in the motor cortex modulate their activity when there is a change in force production, but less so when the constant force is maintained over time.
source: This idea would account for the observation that neurons in the motor cortex modulate their activity when there is a change in force production, but less so when the constant force is maintained over time (Shalit et al., 2012; Georgopoulos et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: To maintain a constant force over time, a subcortical area integrates phasic activity from the cortex, and maintains its output over time.
source: To maintain a constant force over time, our conjecture states that a subcortical area integrates phasic activity from the cortex, and maintains its output over time.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Transient stimulation of the brainstem in decerebrate cats produces sustained (timescale of minutes) changes in extensor muscle force.
source: This idea is consistent with evidence that transient stimulation of the brainstem in decerebrate cats produces sustained (timescale of minutes) changes in extensor muscle force (Mori et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Equation 1 describes how the integration of move activity may relate to changes in hold commands, but does not specify the hold command at the target.
source: Equations (1) and (2) describe how the integration of move activity may relate to changes in hold commands, but does not specify the hold command at the target.
evidence: This is a limitation of the mathematical model.

claim: Move period commands alone will not determine the terminal position of the arm: the initial arm position must also be taken into account.
source: This reflects the reality that move period commands alone will not determine the terminal position of the arm: the initial arm position must also be taken into account.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for postural control.

claim: To hold the limb at the target, the integrator must not only integrate move commands, it must add this integral to the hold period activity that preceded movement.
source: In other words, to hold the limb at the target, the integrator must not only integrate move commands, it must add this integral to the hold period activity that preceded movement (see Equation (6) in Materials and methods; illustrated in Figure 7G).
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement illustrated in the model.

claim: It is not obvious why the linear functions in Equations 1 and 2 robustly predicted the relationship between change in hold activity and the integral of move activity without a biomechanical model of the arm.
source: Without a biomechanical model of the arm, it is not obvious why the linear functions in Equations (1) and (2) robustly predicted the relationship between change in hold activity and the integral of move activity.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in understanding the mechanism.

claim: The motor cortex likely has some role in postural control, at least through monosynaptic projections from corticomotoneurons to alpha-motoneurons in the spinal cord.
source: It is unlikely that the motor cortex has no role in postural control. At the very least, the monosynaptic projections from corticomotoneurons (Griffin et al., 2015) to alpha-motoneurons in the spinal cord are likely to be active during periods of holding still.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on anatomical knowledge and a citation.

claim: Hold period signals in the cortex may arise from recurrent connections with a subcortical integration system, or from a separate position controller.
source: We do not know if these hold period signals in the cortex arise from recurrent connections with a subcortical integration system, or from a separate position controller.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the neural mechanisms.

claim: Understanding the differential contributions of cortical systems and the putative subcortical integrator is essential to improve understanding of neurological disorders such as stroke and dystonia.
source: Understanding the differential contributions of the cortical systems and the putative subcortical integrator is essential to improve our understanding of neurological disorders such as stroke and dystonia (Sadnicka et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical relevance of the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Abnormal postures at rest in stroke and dystonia patients could arise from a lesion to the integrator circuit, or from the normal integration of chronically abnormal moving commands.
source: Identifying the locus of the reach integration may help explain why these patients exhibit abnormal postures at rest. These abnormalities could arise from a lesion to the integrator circuit, or perhaps more provocatively, from the normal integration of chronically abnormal moving commands.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanisms of clinical symptoms.
